issues.legal_issue: The government must give existing licensed traders preference in allotting premises in a newly established market when the new market requires them to shift their trade there.
material_facts: The traders had conducted business for many years in existing market areas.
The government established new market townships, and traders needed to conduct their agricultural-produce business at the new markets.
The government proposed allotting plots and buildings through open auction without giving existing traders any preference.
The government acknowledged that sufficient space was available to accommodate the existing traders.
issues.conclusion: The existing licensed traders must receive preference in the allotment of buildings or plots in the new markets; merely allowing them to compete in an open auction does not discharge the government's obligation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(1) and 3(2) of the Punjab New Mandi Township (Development and Regulation) Act, 1960, the government may create a new mandi and transfer its land or buildings by auction, allotment, or otherwise. Rule 3, made under Section 3(2) and Section 25(a), permits sale by public auction or allotment. Section 4 restricts use or occupation of buildings and sites without the administrator's written permission, leaving traders dependent on authorized allotments. The Court affirmed the principle in M/s Prem Chand Trilok Chand v. State of Haryana that the government has an inherent obligation to provide sufficient accommodation for licensed dealers when it regulates the place of sale, and rejected Chand Ram Ram Chand v. State of Punjab insofar as it treated an opportunity to compete as sufficient. Equal competition was not enough because existing traders already had the same opportunity as the public without a special provision.

issues.definition: When a new-market allotment dispute concerns existing licensed traders who must shift their trade to the new market, sufficient premises are available, and an open auction offers only equal competition, the traders must receive preference in allotment.

issues.legal_issue: Preference for existing licensed traders in a newly established market does not require free allotment or allotment below the reserved price, and any preferential price must not be unreasonable.
material_facts: The government was allotting land and buildings in newly established markets to traders who had to conduct their agricultural-produce business there.
The government contended that allotment could be through open auction and sought to earn revenue.
The Court considered the government's statutory powers to allot or transfer land and buildings and the existing traders' need for premises in the new markets.
issues.conclusion: The government need not allot premises free of charge or below the reserved price; it may set a price above the reserved price for preferential allotment, provided the price is not unreasonable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Punjab New Mandi Township (Development and Regulation) Act, 1960, and Rule 3, made under Section 3(2) and Section 25(a), allow transfer by allotment as well as public auction. The government may set an allotment price having regard to market price, but its broad discretion must account for the handicaps faced by existing traders and may not be exercised to their detriment. The Court clarified that the preference required by M/s Prem Chand Trilok Chand v. State of Haryana does not mean free allotment or a price below the reserved price; a higher price is permissible if it is not unreasonable.
